name: The Pawn Fork
summary: A pawn fork attacks two enemy pieces with a single pawn move; here 1.d5 strikes Black's knights on c6 and e6 at once, winning one of them.
intro: The pawn fork is the humblest member of the fork family: one pawn move that attacks two enemy pieces at the same time. Because a pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it, any two enemy pieces sitting on those squares are hit simultaneously. The defender can usually save only one of them, and trading a piece for a mere pawn is almost never acceptable, so material is lost. In the diagram, White's modest d4-pawn is poised to demonstrate exactly this idea against Black's two knights.
boardCaption: White to move: the d4-pawn advances with 1.d5, attacking both Black knights on c6 and e6 at the same time.

sections.heading: The Cheapest Fork
paragraphs: What makes the pawn fork so effective is the attacker's price tag. A pawn is the cheapest unit on the board, so when it attacks a knight, bishop, rook, or queen, the threatened piece must move; capturing the pawn would mean giving up far more material than it costs. When one pawn move creates two such threats at once, the defender faces an impossible arithmetic: two valuable pieces are attacked, and only one can be rescued per move.

This is the essence of every double attack, distilled to its simplest form. The opponent almost never wants to trade a piece for a pawn, and there is rarely a single move that defends or relocates both targets. Unlike a knight fork or queen fork, no clever escape by counterattack is usually available against so cheap an aggressor, which is why even beginners can win material outright the moment the pattern appears.

sections.heading: The Example
paragraphs: In the diagram, White has a pawn on d4 while Black's knights stand on c6 and e6. White plays 1.d5, advancing the pawn one square. A white pawn on d5 attacks the squares c6 and e6 diagonally, so this single quiet-looking push assaults both knights simultaneously. Neither knight can capture the pawn without losing itself for almost nothing, and no reply can shelter both pieces at once.

Black must choose which knight to save. In our line the e6-knight steps aside with 1...Nc5, escaping the attack. But the knight on c6 remains under fire, and White simply collects it with 2.dxc6, winning a whole piece for the pawn's trouble. The sequence could hardly be shorter: one advance, one forced concession, one capture, and White emerges a knight ahead.

sections.heading: Setting Up a Pawn Fork
paragraphs: The geometry is strict and therefore easy to memorize. A pawn attacks only the two squares diagonally ahead of it, so the two victims must sit side by side, exactly two files apart, on the rank just in front of the square the pawn can reach. A very common shape is a pawn pushing to the fifth rank and hitting two enemy minor pieces posted on the sixth, just as 1.d5 does here.

Train your eye to scan for this alignment in both directions. When two of your opponent's pieces settle two files apart on the same rank, check whether one of your pawns can advance to the square between and beneath them. Equally, before parking your own knights and bishops on adjacent outposts, ask whether an enemy pawn push can fork them; many pieces are lost not to brilliant combinations but to this simplest of tactical patterns.

keyIdeas: A pawn fork is one pawn move that attacks two enemy pieces at the same time.
Because the pawn is the cheapest unit, the opponent can almost never afford to capture it with a piece.
Only one attacked piece can usually be saved per move, so the other is lost.
A pawn attacks just the two squares diagonally in front of it, so fork victims stand two files apart on the rank ahead.
A typical pattern is a push to the fifth rank forking two minor pieces on the sixth, as with 1.d5 against knights on c6 and e6.
Scan every pawn advance, yours and your opponent's, for the two-files-apart alignment before placing pieces side by side.
